question: Company A in perfect competition and Company B a monopolist both earn Rs 100cr EBITDA. Which should trade at higher PE and why?
before: Monopolist earnings protected by barriers and no competitors -- more durable. In perfect competition, supernormal profits attract entrants until margins go to zero. A EBITDA is at risk of being competed away. Market pays premium for certainty and sustainability.
after:
Concept: In perfect competition, firms earn normal profits in long-run equilibrium because free entry erodes supernormal returns. A monopolist protected by barriers to entry can sustain supernormal profits indefinitely. When two firms report identical current earnings (Rs 100cr EBITDA), the market values them differently based on the durability and sustainability of those earnings streams.

Why this is correct: Company B (monopolist) should trade at a higher PE multiple because its earnings are structurally protected by barriers to entry—such as patents, switching costs, network effects, or regulatory moats. Company A's Rs 100cr EBITDA will attract new entrants in perfect competition, eroding margins until only normal returns remain. Equity analysts assign higher multiples to sustainable, durable earnings. The monopolist's competitive moat makes its current EBITDA more likely to persist, whereas the competitor's identical EBITDA is temporary.

Why the others are wrong: A misinterprets competitive efficiency as a reason for higher valuation—while competitive markets are dynamically efficient, that efficiency is precisely why supernormal profits are competed away, making current earnings unreliable. C ignores the fundamental principle that PE multiples reflect expected future earnings, not current earnings alone; identical EBITDA today does not imply identical expected future EBITDA when one firm faces competitive pressure and the other does not. D is unnecessarily defeatist; the microeconomic structure of each market provides sufficient information to rank earnings quality and sustainability.

Intuition: Equity research distinguishes between reported earnings and sustainable earnings power. A rupee of monopoly EBITDA is worth more than a rupee of competitive EBITDA because it is more likely to persist into future years and support higher distributions. Barriers to entry translate directly into multiple expansion in the market—this is why moat analysis is central to equity valuation.
